_comment: Numbers the app shows as figures rather than prose. Source ids match the numbered list in banana_stages.md ('## Sources and references'). Written in plain, everyday English: the people reading it in the app are not nutritionists. Edit here, not in the app.
basis: These figures are for 100 g of banana. A medium banana weighs about 118 g, so it holds a bit more.

prebiotic_explainer.what: A prebiotic is food for the good bacteria living in your gut. You can't digest it yourself, so it reaches them whole [14].
prebiotic_explainer.how: This kind of starch, and the pectin alongside it, pass through your stomach untouched. Once they reach your large intestine, your gut bacteria eat them and make butyrate — the main fuel for the cells lining your gut [15][6].
prebiotic_explainer.why: How much a banana carries depends on how ripe it is. Ripening turns that starch into sugar, so the greener the banana, the more there is for your gut [2][3].

unripe.level_label: The best stage for your gut
unripe.headline_label: of fibre your body can't digest, in 100 g
unripe.summary: A green banana is the best one you can eat for your gut. It holds about 18 g of fibre in every 100 g — that's about two thirds of what you need in a whole day, and roughly four times what a yellow banana has [2][16].
unripe.gut: Your body can't break this down, so it reaches your large intestine whole and your gut bacteria feed on it [6][15]. If you are eating bananas for your gut, pick this one.

facts.label: Can upset a sensitive gut
facts.note: a firm green banana is usually fine up to about 100 g

ripe.headline_label: of fibre your body can't digest, in 100 g
ripe.summary: Once a banana turns yellow, most of that starch has become sugar. The fibre drops to about 4 to 5 g in every 100 g — roughly a sixth of what you need in a day — while the sugar climbs to about 15 g [2][16].
ripe.gut: There is still something here for your gut bacteria to feed on [6][15], but only a fraction of what a green banana gives them. A firm yellow banana keeps more of it than a spotted one [2].

facts.label: Can upset a sensitive gut
facts.note: harder to handle once brown spots show up

overripe.level_label: Almost none left for your gut
overripe.headline_label: of fibre your body can't digest, in 100 g
overripe.summary: A banana covered in brown spots has turned nearly all its starch into sugar. The fibre falls to about 2 g in every 100 g — less than a tenth of what you need in a day, and about a ninth of what a green banana has [2][16].
overripe.gut: There is very little left for your gut bacteria to feed on [2][3]. This banana is at its sweetest and has the most antioxidants, but for your gut it is the weakest stage.

facts.label: Can upset a sensitive gut
facts.note: keep to a small piece if bananas usually bother you

rotten.headline_label: throw it away or put it in the compost
rotten.summary: There is no point weighing up the gut benefit of a banana that has gone off. Soft, mouldy fruit should be thrown out whole, because the mould grows down into it and you can't see how far [9].
rotten.gut: Whatever fibre is left is not worth the risk of the poisons mould can make [8][9]. Compost this one and scan a fresher banana.

baseline.title: Every banana, any stage
baseline.note: USDA lists one set of figures for raw banana whatever its stage, so these stay about the same as it ripens [1][2].

rows.label: Carbs
rows.note: starch turns into sugar as it ripens
